See Maundrell, A Journey from Aleppo to Jerusalem.

Procopius, Anecdota, c. 11. Theophanes, Chronographia, p. 122. John Malalas, Chronographia, tom. II, p. 62. I remember an observation, half philosophical, half superstitious, that the province which had been ruined by the bigotry of Justinian was the same through which the Muhammadans penetrated into the empire.
The expression of Procopius is remarkable: οὐ γἀρ οι ἐδόκει φόνος ἀνθρώπων εἶναι, ἢν γε μὴ τῆς αὐτοῦ δόξης οἰ τελευτῶντες τὐχοιεν ὄντες. Anecdota, c. 13.

See the Chronicle of Victor, p. 328, and the original evidence of the laws of Justinian. During the first years of his reign, Baronius himself is in extreme good humor with the emperor, who courted the popes till he got them into his power.
Procopius, Anecdota, c. 13. Evagrius, l. IV c. 10. If the ecclesiastical never read the secret historian, their common suspicion proves at least the general hatred.

On the subject of the three chapters, the original acts of the fifth general council of Constantinople supply much useless, though authentic, knowledge (Sacrosancta concilia, tom. VI, pp. 1⁠–⁠419). The Greek Evagrius is less copious and correct (l. IV c. 38) than the three zealous Africans, Facundus (in his twelve books, Pro defensione trium capitulorum, which are most correctly published by Sirmond), Liberatus (in his Breviarium causae Nestorianorum, c. 22⁠–⁠24), and Victor Tunnunensis in his Chronicle (in tom. I Lectiones antiquae Canisii 330⁠–⁠334). The Liber pontificalis, or Anastasius (in “Vigilio,” “Pelagio,” etc.), is original Italian evidence. The modern reader will derive some information from Dupin (Bibliothèque ecclésiastique, tom. V, pp. 189⁠–⁠207) and Basnage (Histoire de l’Eglise, tom. I, pp. 519⁠–⁠541); yet the latter is too firmly resolved to depreciate the authority and character of the popes.

Origen had indeed too great a propensity to imitate the πλάνη and δυσσέβεια of the old philosophers (Justinian, ad Mennam, in Sacrosancta concilia, tom. VI, p. 356). His moderate opinions were too repugnant to the zeal of the church, and he was found guilty of the heresy of treason.

Basnage (Praefatio, pp. 11⁠–⁠14, ad tom. I Lectiones antiquae Canisii) has fairly weighed the guilt and innocence of Theodore of Mopsuestia. If he composed 10,000 volumes, as many errors would be a charitable allowance. In all the subsequent catalogues of heresiarchs, he alone, without his two brethren, is included; and it is the duty of Asseman (Bibliotheca orientalis, tom. IV, pp. 203⁠–⁠207) to justify the sentence.

See the complaints of Liberatus and Victor, and the exhortations of Pope Pelagius to the conqueror and exarch of Italy. Schisma⁠ ⁠… per potestates publicas opprimatur, etc. (Sacrosancta concilia, tom. VI, p. 467, etc.). An army was detained to suppress the sedition of an Illyrian city. See Procopius (De bello Gothico, l. IV c. 25): ὦνπερ ἔνεκα σφίσιν αὐτοῖς οί Χριστιανοι διαμάχονται. He seems to promise an ecclesiastical history. It would have been curious and impartial.

The bishops of the patriarchate of Aquileia were reconciled by Pope Honorius, AD 638 (Muratori, Annali d’Italia, tom. V, p. 376); but they again relapsed, and the schism was not finally extinguished till 698. Fourteen years before, the church of Spain had overlooked the fifth general council with contemptuous silence (XIII Concilium Toletanum in Sacrosancta concilia, tom. VII, pp. 487⁠–⁠494).

Nicetius, bishop of Treves (Sacrosancta concilia, tom. VI, pp. 511⁠–⁠513). He himself, like most of the Gallican prelates (Gregorii, Epistulae, l. VII “Epistula 5” in Sacrosancta concilia, tom. VI, p. 1007), was separated from the communion of the four patriarchs by his refusal to condemn the three chapters. Baronius almost pronounces the damnation of Justinian (“AD 565,” No. 6).

After relating the last heresy of Justinian (l. IV c. 39⁠–⁠41) and the edict of his successor (l. V c. 3), the remainder of the history of Evagrius is filled with civil, instead of ecclesiastical, events.

This extraordinary and perhaps inconsistent doctrine of the Nestorians had been observed by La Croze (Histoire du christianisme des Indes, tom. I, pp. 19, 20), and is more fully exposed by Abulpharagius (Bibliotheca orientalis, tom. II, p. 292; Historia compendiosa dynastiarum, p. 91, vers. Latin, Pococke) and Asseman himself (tom. IV, p. 218). They seem ignorant that they might allege the positive authority of the Ecthesis. Ὁ μιαρὸς Νεστόριος καίπερ διαιρῶν τὴν θείαν τοῦ Κυρίου ἐνανθρώπησιν, καὶ δύο είσάγων υἰούς (the common reproach of the Monophysites), δύο θελήματα τούτων εἰπεῖν οὐκ ἐτόλμησε, τοὐναντίον δὲ ταύτοβουλίαν τῶν⁠ ⁠… δύο προσώπων ἐδόξασε (Sacrosancta concilia, tom. VII, p. 205).

See the Orthodox faith in Petavius (Dogmata theologica, tom. V l. IX c. 6⁠–⁠10, pp. 433⁠–⁠447): all the depths of this controversy are sounded in the Greek dialogue between Maximus and Pyrrhus (ad calcem Baronius, tom. VIII Annales ecclesiastici, pp. 755⁠–⁠794), which relates a real conference, and produced as short-lived a conversion.

Impiissimam ecthesim⁠ ⁠… scelerosum typum (Sacrosancta concilia, tom. VII, p. 366), diabolicae operationis genimina (fors. germina, or else the Greek γενήματα, in the original; Sacrosancta concilia, pp. 363, 364) are the expressions of the eighteenth anathema. The epistle of Pope Martin to Amandus, Gallican bishop, stigmatizes the Monothelites and their heresy with equal virulence (p. 392).

The sufferings of Martin and Maximus are described with simplicity in their original letters and acts (Sacrosancta concilia, tom. VII, pp. 63⁠–⁠78; Baronius, Annales ecclesiastici, “AD 656,” No. 2, et annos subsequent). Yet the chastisement of their disobedience, ἐξορία and σώματος αἰκισμός, had been previously announced in the Type of Constans (Sacrosancta concilia, tom. VII, p. 240).

Eutychius (Annales, tom. II, p. 368) most erroneously supposes that the 124 bishops of the Roman synod transported themselves to Constantinople; and by adding them to the 168 Greeks, thus composes the sixth council of 292 fathers.

The Monothelite Constans was hated by all διἀ τοι ταῦτα (says Theophanes, Chronographia, p. 292) ἐμισήθη σφόδρῶς παρὰ πάντων. When the Monothelite monk failed in his miracle, the people shouted ὁ λαός ἀνεβόνησε (Sacrosancta concilia, tom. VII, p. 1032). But this was a natural and transient emotion; and I much fear that the latter is an anticipation of orthodoxy in the good people of Constantinople.

The history of Monothelitism may be found in the Acts of the Synods of Rome (tom. VII, pp. 77⁠–⁠395, 601⁠–⁠608) and Constantinople (pp. 609⁠–⁠1429). Baronius extracted some original documents from the Vatican library; and his chronology is rectified by the diligence of Pagi. Even Dupin (Bibliothèque ecclésiastique, tom. VI, pp. 57⁠–⁠71) and Basnage (Histoire de l’Eglise, tom. I, pp. 541⁠–⁠555) afford a tolerable abridgment.

In the Lateran synod of 679, Wilfred, an Anglo-Saxon bishop, subscribed pro omni Aquilonari parte Britanniae et Hiberniae, quae ab Anglorum et Britonum, necnon Scotorum et Pictorum gentibus colebantur (Eddius, in Vita Sancti Wilfrithi, c. 31, apud Pagi, Critica Baronii, tom. III, p. 88). Theodore (magnae insulae Britanniae archiepiscopus et philosophus) was long expected at Rome (Sacrosancta concilia, tom. VII, p. 714), but he contented himself with holding (AD 680) his provincial synod of Hatfield, in which he received the decrees of Pope Martin and the first Lateran council against the Monothelites (Sacrosancta concilia, tom. VII, p. 597, etc.). Theodore, a monk of Tarsus in Cilicia, had been named to the primacy of Britain by Pope Vitalian (AD 688; see Baronius and Pagi), whose esteem for his learning and piety was tainted by some distrust of his national character⁠—ne quid contrarium veritati fidei, Graecorum more, in ecclesiam cui praeesset introduceret. The Cilician was sent from Rome to Canterbury under the tuition of an African guide (Bedae, Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum, l. IV c. 1). He adhered to the Roman doctrine; and the same creed of the incarnation has been uniformly transmitted from Theodore to the modern primates, whose sound understanding is perhaps seldom engaged with that abstruse mystery.

This name, unknown till the tenth century, appears to be of Syriac origin. It was invented by the Jacobites, and eagerly adopted by the Nestorians and Muhammadans; but it was accepted without shame by the Catholics, and is frequently used in the Annals of Eutychius (Assemani, Bibliotheca orientalis, tom. II, p. 507, etc., tom. III, p. 355; Renaudot, Historia patriarcharum Alexandrinorum, p. 119). Ἡμεῖς δοῦλοι τοῦ βασιλέως, was the acclamation of the fathers of Constantinople (Sacrosancta concilia, tom. VII, p. 765).

I shall not enrich my ignorance with the spoils of Simon, Walton, Mill, Wetstein, Assemani, Ludolphus, La Croze, whom I have consulted with some care. It appears:

In the account of the Monophysites and Nestorians, I am deeply indebted to the Bibliotheca orientalis Clementino-Vaticana of Joseph Simon Assemani. That learned Maronite was despatched in the year 1715 by Pope Clement XI to visit the monasteries of Egypt and Syria, in search of MSS. His four folio volumes, published at Rome 1719⁠–⁠1728, contain a part only, though perhaps the most valuable, of his extensive project. As a native and as a scholar, he possessed the Syriac literature; and though a dependent of Rome, he wishes to be moderate and candid.

See the Arabic canons of Nice in the translation of Abraham Ecchelensis, No. 37⁠–⁠40. Sacrosancta concilia, tom. II, pp. 335, 336, edit. Venetiis. These vulgar titles, Nicene and Arabic, are both apocryphal. The council of Nice enacted no more than twenty canons (Theodoret, Historia ecclesiastica, l. I c. 8), and the remainder, seventy or eighty, were collected from the synods of the Greek church. The Syriac edition of Maruthas is no longer extant (Assemani, Bibliotheca orientalis, tom. I, p. 195, tom. III, p. 74), and the Arabic version is marked with many recent interpolations. Yet this code contains many curious relics of ecclesiastical discipline; and since it is equally revered by all the Eastern communions, it was probably finished before the schism of the Nestorians and Jacobites (Fabricius, Bibliotheca Graeca, tom. XI, pp. 363⁠–⁠367).

Theodore the Reader (l. II c. 5, 49, ad calcem Historia ecclesiastica) has noticed this Persian school of Edessa. Its ancient splendor, and the two eras of its downfall (AD 431 and 489) are clearly discussed by Assemani (Bibliotheca orientalis, tom. II, p. 402, III, pp. 376, 378, IV, pp. 70, 924).

A dissertation on the state of the Nestorians has swelled in the hands of Assemani to a folio volume of 950 pages, and his learned researches are digested in the most lucid order. Besides this fourth volume of the Bibliotheca orientalis, the extracts in the three preceding tomes (tom. I, p. 203, II, pp. 321⁠–⁠463, III 64⁠–⁠70, 378⁠–⁠395, etc., 405⁠–⁠408, 580⁠–⁠589) may be usefully consulted.

See the Topographia christiana of Cosmas, surnamed Indicopleustes, or the Indian navigator, l. III, pp. 178, 179, l. XI, p. 337. The entire work, of which some curious extracts may be found in Photius (codex XXXVI, pp. 9, 10, edit. Hoeschel), Thévenot (in the first part of his Relation de divers voyages, etc.), and Fabricius (Bibliotheca Graeca, l. III c. 25, tom. II, pp. 603⁠–⁠617), has been published by Father Montfaucon at Paris, 1707, in the Collectio nova patrum et scriptorum Graecorum (tom. II, pp. 113⁠–⁠346). It was the design of the author to confute the impious heresy of those who maintained that the earth is a globe, and not a flat oblong table, as it is represented in the Scriptures (l. II, p. 138). But the nonsense of the monk is mingled with the practical knowledge of the traveller, who performed his voyage AD 522, and published his book at Alexandria, AD 547 (l. II, pp. 140, 141. Montfaucon, Praefatio c. 2). The Nestorianism of Cosmas, unknown to his learned editor, was detected by La Croze (Histoire du christianisme des Indes, tom. I, pp. 40⁠–⁠55), and is confirmed by Assemani (Bibliotheca orientalis, tom. IV, pp. 605, 606).

In its long progress to Mosul, Jerusalem, Rome, etc., the story of Prester John evaporated in a monstrous fable, of which some features have been borrowed from the Lama of Tibet (Histoire généalogique des Tatars, partie II, p. 42; Histoire du Grand Genghizcan, p. 31, etc.), and were ignorantly transferred by the Portuguese to the emperor of Abyssinia (Ludolphus, Historia et commentarius Aethiopica, l. II c. 1). Yet it is probable that in the eleventh and twelth centuries Nestorian Christianity was professed in the horde of the Keraites (d’Herbelot, pp. 256, 915, 959; Assemani, tom. IV, pp. 468⁠–⁠504).

The Christianity of China, between the seventh and the thirteenth century, is invincibly proved by the consent of Chinese, Arabian, Syriac, and Latin evidence (Assemani, Bibliotheca orientalis, tom. IV, pp. 502⁠–⁠552; Mémoires de l’Académie des inscriptions, tom. XXX, pp. 802⁠–⁠819). The inscription of Siganfu, which describes the fortunes of the Nestorian church, from the first mission, AD 636, to the current year 781, is accused of forgery by La Croze, Voltaire, etc., who become the dupes of their own cunning, while they are afraid of a Jesuitical fraud.

Jacobitae et Nestorianae plures quam Graeci et Latini. Jacobitae Vitriaco, Historia Hierosolymitana, l. II c. 76, p. 1093, in the Gesta Dei per Francos. The numbers are given by Thomassin, Discipline de l’église, tom. I, p. 172.

The division of the patriarchate may be traced in the Bibliotheca orientalis of Assemani, tom. I, pp. 523⁠–⁠549, tom. II, p. 457, etc.; tom. III, pp. 603, 621⁠–⁠623; tom. IV, pp. 164⁠–⁠169, 423, 622⁠–⁠629, etc.

The pompous language of Rome, on the submission of a Nestorian patriarch, is elegantly represented in the seventh book of Fra Paola: Babylon, Nineveh, Arbela, and the trophies of Alexander, Tauris and Ecbatana, the Tigris and Indus.

The Indian missionary St. Thomas, an apostle, a Manichaean, or an Armenian merchant (La Croze, Histoire du christianisme des Indes, tom. I, pp. 57⁠–⁠70), was famous, however, as early as the time of Jerome (ad Marcellam, “Epistola 148”). Marco-Polo was informed on the spot that he suffered martyrdom in the city of Malabar, or Meliapour, a league only from Madras (d’Anville, Éclaircissemens géographiques sur l’Inde, p. 125), where the Portuguese founded an episcopal church under the name of St. Thomé, and where the saint performed an annual miracle, till he was silenced by the profane neighborhood of the English (La Croze, tom. II, pp. 7⁠–⁠16).

Neither the author of the Saxon Chronicle (AD 833) not William of Malmesbury (De gestis regum Anglorum, l. The three Protestant historians, Ludolphus (Historia aethiopica, Francofurti ad Maenum, 1681; Commentarius, 1691; Relatio Nova, etc., 1693, in folio), Geddes (Church History of Aethiopia, London, 1696, in octavo), and La Croze (Histoire du christianisme d’Ethiopie et d’Arménie, La Haye, 1739, in duodecimo), have drawn their principal materials from the Jesuits, especially from the General History of Baltazar Tellez, published in Portuguese at Coimbra, 1660. We might be surprised at their frankness; but their most flagitious vice, the spirit of persecution, was in their eyes the most meritorious virtue. Ludolphus possessed some, though a slight, advantage from the Aethiopic language, and the personal conversation of Gregory, a free-spirited Abyssinian priest, whom he invited from Rome to the court of Saxe-Gotha.
